p.x:
At our school, every student learns the same internet rules.
Rule 1: Keep your password secret. Don't tell it to your friends. Only your parent can know it.
Rule 2: Don't share personal information. Never write your full name, your home address or your age on a website or game.
Rule 3: Be careful with strangers. Some people online are not who they say they are. If a stranger asks to meet you, tell an adult immediately.
Rule 4: Don't click on pop-ups or open spam emails. They can give your computer a virus.
Rule 5: Be kind. Never bully other people online. If someone is unkind to you, take a screenshot and show it to a teacher.
Rule 6: If a website asks for a login code from your phone, ask an adult first. Some hackers try to hack children's game accounts this way.

Every day, millions of people receive messages from scammers. Some are easy to recognise, but others look very real. Here are some warning signs.
First, check the sender. A phishing email may look like it comes from your bank, but the address is often strange, such as 'k-bank-help123@mail.com'. Real banks never ask you to send your password by email.
Second, be suspicious of urgent messages. Scammers often say, "Your account will be closed in 24 hours!" to make you panic.
Third, don't open attachments or click links unless you are sure they are safe. They may contain malware, which can steal your files or your bank details. This is how identity theft often begins.
Finally, protect your devices. Use antivirus software, keep your firewall turned on and update your apps regularly. If you're not sure whether a message is real, verify it by calling the company directly.
Young people face other dangers, too. Some are cyberbullied by classmates, and this can be very harmful. If it happens to you or a friend, talk to someone you trust.

Each time we search the web, post a photo or use a free app, we leave a trail of data behind us. This digital footprint can reveal a surprising amount: where we live, who our friends are, what we buy and even what we believe. Much of this information is collected legally, often with our consent, buried in long terms and conditions that few people read.
The risks are not only commercial. When a company suffers a data breach, criminals may gain access to millions of passwords and personal records. Hackers frequently exploit a single vulnerability in widely used software, and stolen data can be sold, used to impersonate victims or used to make fraudulent purchases. In the worst cases, criminals use private images to blackmail people.
There are, fortunately, simple ways to reduce the danger. Two-factor authentication, which requires a code from a second device in addition to a password, blocks the vast majority of attacks on personal accounts. Messaging apps that encrypt conversations from end to end make it far harder for anyone, including the app company, to read them. And before entering details on a website, it is worth checking that it is legitimate.
The question of government surveillance is more controversial. Supporters argue that monitoring online activity helps prevent crime and terrorism; critics fear that it threatens freedom of expression. Most experts agree that, whatever the balance, citizens deserve to know what data is being collected about them and why.
